topic: Chemical cells and fuel cells (chemistry only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: A chemical cell is connected to a lamp and the lamp lights. Where does the electricity come from?
items.correct: From chemicals inside the cell that react together
items.misconception: From electricity stored in the cell already
items.why: Everyday language treats batteries as full or empty, and circuit diagrams show charge flowing out of the cell, which invites the picture of a tank being emptied. Cells contain chemicals which react to produce electricity. Nothing flows until the circuit is complete; the reaction then produces the electricity.
items.random_wrong: From a store of electrons in the metal casing

items.q: Two cells are identical except that one uses zinc and copper electrodes and the other uses magnesium and copper. The cells give different voltages. Why?
items.correct: The voltage depends on the type of electrode used
items.misconception: The voltage depends on how much electrolyte there is
items.why: Students conflate voltage with how long a cell lasts. A larger cell does hold more reactant and so lasts longer, which is read as being more powerful. The voltage produced by a cell is dependent upon factors including the type of electrode and electrolyte. Size affects lifetime and current, not the voltage.
items.random_wrong: The voltage depends on the area of the electrode

items.q: A simple cell uses zinc and copper electrodes in copper sulfate solution. The copper sulfate solution is replaced by a different electrolyte, with everything else unchanged. What happens to the voltage?
items.correct: It may change, as the voltage depends on electrolyte
items.misconception: It stays the same, because only the metals matter here
items.why: Students latch onto a single metal in the pair, usually the more reactive one, instead of comparing the two, and reverse the direction of the trend. The voltage rises as the difference in reactivity of the two metals rises. A metal only just above copper in the reactivity series gives a small voltage with copper.
items.random_wrong: It stays the same for any liquid, even for pure water

items.q: Which pair of electrodes, dipped into an electrolyte, would produce a voltage?
items.correct: A zinc strip and a copper strip
items.misconception: Two identical strips of copper metal
items.why: Electrolysis is met first, where two identical carbon or platinum electrodes are normal, so students carry that arrangement over to cells. A simple cell can be made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte. Identical electrodes react with the electrolyte in the same way, so there is no voltage.
items.random_wrong: Two copper strips of different size

items.q: A battery is made by connecting four 1.5 V cells together in series. What voltage does the battery provide, and why?
items.correct: 6.0 V, because the voltages of the cells add up
items.misconception: 1.5 V, because the cells share one voltage
items.why: In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere and the supply voltage is shared between the components, and this sharing rule is applied to the cells themselves. Batteries consist of two or more cells connected together in series to provide a greater voltage. Four 1.5 V cells give 6.0 V.
items.random_wrong: 6.0 V, because the current from each cell adds

items.q: A non-rechargeable cell stops producing a voltage after some time in use. Why does it stop?
items.correct: One of the reactants has been completely used up
items.misconception: All the electrons inside the cell have been used up
items.why: The tank model of a battery survives into this topic: the cell is imagined as a store of charge that empties with use. In non-rechargeable cells and batteries the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up.
items.random_wrong: The electrolyte has leaked out of its case

items.q: Which statement about alkaline batteries is correct?
items.correct: They are non-rechargeable, so they are replaced
items.misconception: They can be recharged from the mains many times over
items.why: Advertising stresses how long alkaline cells last, and rechargeable AA cells look identical to alkaline AA cells on the shelf. The specification states that alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable: their reactions cannot be reversed, so they are replaced when flat.
items.random_wrong: They are rechargeable once the alkali is replaced

items.q: A rechargeable cell is connected to an external electrical supply. What happens inside the cell?
items.correct: The chemical reactions are reversed
items.misconception: Fresh reactants are pushed into the cell
items.why: 'Recharge' shares its everyday meaning with refilling a tank, and students have no picture of a reaction being driven backwards. Rechargeable cells and batteries can be recharged because the chemical reactions are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied.
items.random_wrong: Extra electrons are stored inside it

items.q: Cells are made from a copper electrode and one other metal in the same electrolyte. The voltages are: magnesium 2.7 V, zinc 1.1 V, iron 0.8 V. Tin is less reactive than iron but more reactive than copper. What voltage would a tin and copper cell most likely give?
items.correct: About 0.5 V, because tin is close to copper in reactivity
items.misconception: About 1.9 V, from the zinc and iron values added
items.why: Data questions invite arithmetic, so students combine the numbers in front of them rather than reasoning from the reactivity order. Adding the values is always wrong. If both cells share the same second electrode, the difference between two values gives the cell made from the other two metals (2.7 V - 1.1 V = 1.6 V for magnesium and zinc). For a metal that is not in the table, use its position in the reactivity series instead.
items.random_wrong: About 3.4 V, since tin is the least reactive metal

items.q: Where does the hydrogen in a hydrogen fuel cell come from?
items.correct: It is fed in from an external supply of the fuel
items.misconception: It is stored inside the cell when the cell is built
items.why: Fuel cells are met immediately after rechargeable cells, and both are drawn as a box in a circuit, so the external fuel supply is overlooked. Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel (eg hydrogen) and oxygen or air. Nothing is stored in the cell and no recharging is involved.
items.random_wrong: It is made inside the cell from air and water

items.q: In a hydrogen fuel cell, how does the fuel produce a potential difference?
items.correct: It is oxidised electrochemically at an electrode
items.misconception: It is burned, and the heat drives a generator
items.why: Hydrogen is known as a fuel that burns, and the only familiar way of getting electricity from a fuel is to burn it in a power station. The fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the fuel cell to produce a potential difference; there is no burning and no generator.
items.random_wrong: It is reduced by oxygen at the negative electrode

items.q: Which equation represents the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell?
items.misconception: H2 + O2 → H2O + O
items.why: Balancing is treated as making the totals agree by any available means, and students who alter the right-hand side often do not go back and re-check the left. Put numbers in front of the formulae, then count every element on both sides: H2 + O2 → 2H2O leaves the hydrogen unbalanced. Writing H2O + O does make the atoms tally, but it invents a lone oxygen atom that is not a product, so it is still wrong.

items.q: Why are hydrogen fuel cells described as a potential alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries?
items.correct: They keep working while hydrogen is supplied, with no recharging
items.misconception: They can be refilled with electricity at any charge point
items.why: Fuel cells are met immediately after rechargeable cells, and both are drawn as a box in a circuit, so the external fuel supply is overlooked. Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel (eg hydrogen) and oxygen or air. Nothing is stored in the cell and no recharging is involved.
items.random_wrong: They store far more electricity inside them than a battery

items.q: A car maker compares a hydrogen fuel cell car with a rechargeable battery car. Which is a genuine disadvantage of the fuel cell car?
items.correct: Hydrogen is difficult to store safely
items.misconception: It gives out carbon dioxide as it is driven
items.why: Every fuel students have met, from methane to petrol, contains carbon, so carbon dioxide is treated as the automatic product of any fuel. Hydrogen contains no carbon, so the cell produces only water. Carbon dioxide may be released elsewhere, when the hydrogen is manufactured.
items.random_wrong: It must be plugged in and recharged often

items.q: (HT) A hydrogen fuel cell has an acidic electrolyte. Which half equation shows the reaction at the negative electrode?
items.why: Balancing is treated as making the totals agree by any available means, and students who alter the right-hand side often do not go back and re-check the left. Put numbers in front of the formulae, then count every element on both sides: H2 + O2 → 2H2O leaves the hydrogen unbalanced. Writing H2O + O does make the atoms tally, but it invents a lone oxygen atom that is not a product, so it is still wrong.

items.q: (HT) A hydrogen fuel cell has an acidic electrolyte. Which half equation shows the reaction at the positive electrode?
items.why: H2O2 looks like a reasonable product from H2 and O2, and 'fuel' is associated with the carbon dioxide given off by burning petrol. The overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell involves the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

items.q: A games controller is used every day and flattens its cells within a week. Which is the best reason for choosing rechargeable cells for it?
items.correct: They can be reused many times, so fewer cells are bought
items.misconception: Recharging pushes new chemicals in, so they never wear out
items.why: 'Recharge' shares its everyday meaning with refilling a tank, and students have no picture of a reaction being driven backwards. Rechargeable cells and batteries can be recharged because the chemical reactions are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied.
items.random_wrong: They hold much more electricity inside them when new

items.q: Does using thicker connecting wire change the voltage of a cell?
items.correct: No. The voltage comes from the reaction between the chemicals, not from the circuit outside the cell.
items.misconception: The voltage is a property of the circuit and the wires, so changing the connections changes the voltage.
items.why: Voltage is first met as something measured across components in a circuit, so it is attached to the circuit rather than to the chemistry that generates it. The voltage is set by the type of electrode and electrolyte. The external wire only provides a path for the current.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Would zinc and copper in pure water make a working cell?
items.correct: No. Pure water has almost no ions to carry charge, so it does not act as an electrolyte.
items.misconception: Any liquid will do as the electrolyte, because the current just needs something to travel through.
items.why: Diagrams show the metals in a beaker of clear liquid, and students see the liquid as a gap-filler rather than as a chemical taking part. A simple cell needs two different metals in contact with an electrolyte, and the type of electrolyte affects the voltage produced.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a large copper strip with a small copper strip a simple cell?
items.correct: No. The electrodes must be different metals, not the same metal in different sizes.
items.misconception: 'Two different electrodes' means two electrodes that differ in some way, such as their size or shape.
items.why: The word 'different' is read loosely, and students know that changing the size of an electrode does change the current, so they assume it changes the voltage too. The specification requires two different metals. Changing the area of an electrode alters the current a cell can supply, not the voltage it produces.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does connecting cells in series give a greater voltage?
items.correct: Because the voltage of each cell adds to the voltage of the next.
items.misconception: Because the current supplied by each cell adds up, and more current means more voltage.
items.why: Current and voltage are not clearly separated, so any statement about 'more' from more cells is expressed in terms of current. Cells in series provide a greater voltage. The current through cells in series is the same through each one; it is the voltages that add.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must every reactant be used up before a cell stops working?
items.correct: No. The reactions stop as soon as one of the reactants has been used up.
items.misconception: A cell keeps going until everything inside it, both electrodes and the electrolyte, has been used up.
items.why: Students picture the cell running down evenly, rather than one reactant running out first while the rest is left unreacted. The chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up; the other reactants are simply left over.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is hydrogen oxidised or reduced in a hydrogen fuel cell?
items.correct: Oxidised. Hydrogen gains oxygen inside the cell to form water.
items.misconception: Hydrogen is reduced, because it combines with oxygen and gains something.
items.why: Oxidation is remembered as 'gaining oxygen', but the gain is hidden inside the cell, and the word 'reduced' is attached to the fuel because the fuel is used up. The fuel is oxidised in a fuel cell and it is the oxygen that is reduced. (HT only: the half equation for the fuel is H2 → 2H+ + 2e−.)
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a hydrogen fuel cell the same as the electrolysis of water?
items.correct: No. Electrolysis uses a current to split water; a fuel cell combines hydrogen and oxygen and supplies a current.
items.misconception: The fuel cell splits water inside itself, or needs a current supplied to it to work.
items.why: The two are taught close together and use the same apparatus in demonstrations, so the direction of the process is confused. A fuel cell is supplied with fuel from outside and produces a potential difference. Electrolysis is the reverse process and consumes electricity.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What must be balanced in a half equation?
items.correct: Both the atoms and the charges on each side.
items.misconception: The number of electrons in a half equation can be chosen freely — you can put in however many you like without making the charges on the two sides balance.
items.why: Electrons are treated as an optional extra written on the end, rather than as charged particles that have to be counted. In H2 → 2H+ + 2e− the two hydrogen atoms balance and the charge is zero on both sides. In O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O the charges also cancel.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which electrode does H2 → 2H+ + 2e− describe?
items.correct: The negative electrode, where hydrogen is oxidised.
items.misconception: The two electrode equations can be swapped, or the acidic and alkaline versions mixed together.
items.why: The two half equations are learned as a pair without being tied to what is happening chemically at each electrode, so their labels and forms get exchanged. At the negative electrode hydrogen loses electrons: H2 → 2H+ + 2e−. At the positive electrode oxygen gains them: O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Once a fuel cell has started, does it need anything supplied to it?
items.correct: Yes. It needs a continuous supply of fuel and of oxygen or air.
items.misconception: Once the reaction has started it keeps itself going and needs nothing further.
items.why: The cell is imagined as being switched on like a battery, so the continuous external supply that defines a fuel cell is forgotten. Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel and oxygen or air. Stop either supply and the cell stops producing a potential difference.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.5.2 Chemical cells and fuel cells (chemistry only)
